'''Timur Magomedovich Eneev''' (September 23, 1924<ref name="Soviet">{{cite web|title=Eneev, Timur Magometovich|url=http://encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com/Timur+Eneev|accessdate=5 August 2013|publisher=[[The Great Soviet Encyclopedia]]}}</ref> – September 8, 2019) was a Russian mathematician specializing in mechanics and control processes. A minor planet Eneev discovered in 1978 is named after him.<ref name="Schmadel2003">{{cite book|author=Lutz Schmadel|title=Dictionary of Minor Planet Names|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VoJ5nUyIzCsC&pg=PA484|accessdate=6 August 2013|date=5 August 2003|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-540-00238-3|pages=484–}}</ref> He was the editor-in-chief of the journal ''[[Cosmic Research]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Cosmic Research|url=https://link.springer.com/journal/10604|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]}}</ref> He was a member of the [[Balkar]] ethnic group.

==Biography==
In 1948 Eneev graduated from the [[Moscow State University]] and until 1953 worked as a research worker at the [[Steklov Institute of Mathematics]]. Since 1953 he is associated with the [[Keldysh Institute of Applied Mathematics]].<ref name="Schmadel2003" />
He became a member of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union|CPSU]] since 1957 and a corresponding member of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences|USSR Academy of Sciences]] in 1968.<ref name="Soviet" />

Eneev received the [[Lenin Prize]] in 1957 and has been awarded the [[Order of Lenin]] and the [[Order of the Red Banner of Labour]].<ref name="Soviet" />
In 2006 he was awarded the prestigious [[Demidov Prize]] of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] in mathematics.
